archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (goaltending-sunk)
archetype.definition: Utah controls 5-on-5 play like one of the league's best teams, but league-worst-tier goaltending and a leaky penalty kill have dragged its results down to a .500-ish goal differential.

report.headline: Elite shot share, bottom-two goaltending: Utah is better than 10-7-1
report.take:
Utah is playing the game it wants to play. Its 5-on-5 expected-goals share of 57.3% ranks 2nd in the league, its shot-attempt share of 54% ranks 5th, and it puts 29.8 shots a game on net while allowing 24.9. Those are contender process numbers. The forwards grade A-, the blueline grades A, and Mikhail Sergachev (5th on the defense tab, 20 points in 24 minutes a night) and Logan Cooley (9th among centers, 11 goals) give the top of the lineup real star power. Add a power play converting 37.1%, 2nd in the league, and a team that out-chances nearly everyone should be well ahead on the scoreboard.

It isn't, because of the crease. The goalies sit at -12.8 GSAx, 31st of 32, with a .871 save percentage, 30th, against a league average of .891. Both Karel Vejmelka (.870, -8.0 GSAx) and Sebastian Cossa (.871, -3.7) are underwater, so this is not one bad starter who can be benched. It is the whole group. The 5-on-5 PDO of 97.3 is the result. Utah's shooting is league-average, so the gap sits almost entirely on the save side. Pair that with a 69.6% penalty kill (27th) and you get a team that allows 3.5 goals a game, 24th, despite allowing fewer shots than most. The upshot is an even goal differential and a 17th-ranked Goal Diff / GP for a team whose chances say top five.

The record itself is roughly honest. Pts vs Goal Diff is +1, so there is no big close-game luck either way. The recent slide is real, though. Over the last 10 Utah is 4-5-1 with a -10 differential, allowing 4.2 a game, and it went 1-3 to open November. Mostly that is the same goaltending problem getting louder rather than the skaters fading. Some warning signs do sit under the surface. Nick Schmaltz is -14 with a 45% xGF share on a top-line workload, and the defense has given up the 26th-most points to opposing defensemen, which fits a penalty kill that keeps getting beaten from the point.

Last season is the reference point. Utah put up 92 points with a +14.1 GSAx and a 52.4% xGF share. This year's skaters are clearly better than last year's, and the goaltending has gone from an asset to a crater. Goaltending at this level rarely stays this bad for 82 games, and the shot share has the look of something real. That makes Utah a likely riser if the saves come back even to average. If they don't, it becomes a wild-card scrapper.

strengths.title: Dominant 5-on-5 territorial control
strengths.body: Utah owns the puck and the quality chances at even strength. It ranks 2nd in expected-goals share and 5th in Corsi, and it outshoots opponents by a healthy margin every night. The depth is broad: Barrett Hayton, Anders Lee, Lawson Crouse and Vincent Trocheck all post xGF shares near or above 60%. Process this strong and this spread across the lineup is the most durable thing on the sheet.

strengths.title: A lethal top-unit power play
strengths.body: At 37.1% the power play ranks 2nd. Keller (15 PP points), Cooley and Schmaltz (12 each) and Sergachev (10) drive it. That conversion rate is far above the league's 22.5% and will come down, but the talent on the unit means it should stay comfortably above average.

strengths.title: Star-level top end
strengths.body: Cooley (21 points, 11 goals) and Keller (24 points) are producing at an elite clip. Sergachev is the 5th-ranked defenseman on the site while logging over 24 minutes a night. Behind them the blueline earns an A with Weegar and Schmidt, so this is not a one-player grade.

concerns.title: Goaltending is giving games away
concerns.body: A -12.8 GSAx ranks 31st, and the team save percentage of .871 is two full points under the league. Both goalies are below expected, so there is no obvious internal fix. Last season the same building got +14.1 GSAx, which argues the current level is partly a bad run. Still, until it turns, Utah needs four goals to feel safe.

concerns.title: A penalty kill that bleeds
concerns.body: At 69.6% the kill ranks 27th and wipes out much of the power play's edge. The defense also gives up points to opposing defensemen at the 26th-worst rate, with an above-league share of the scoring going to D. That points to point shots getting through, a problem worsened by goalies who aren't stopping them.

concerns.title: The slide is getting worse
concerns.body: Over the last 10 Utah is 4-5-1, allowing 4.2 a game with a -10 differential, and it went 1-3 to start November. The offense has dipped only slightly. The damage is on the goals-against side, which ties the slump to the crease rather than to effort or system.

trend.note: A 9-5 October gave way to a 1-3 November start and a -10 differential over the last 10, driven by goals against rather than any drop in shot share.

weekAhead.headline: One tough road test, then three home games versus bottom-feeders
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the hardest game, at Vegas, the site's 5th-ranked team with a 5th-ranked defense and B+ goaltending. Vegas has held opposing centers furthest under expectation of any team in the league, a bad matchup for a Utah attack built through Cooley and Schmaltz. After that the schedule turns friendly: three straight at home against St. Louis (21st), San Jose (28th) and Vancouver (32nd), all with losing records.

The Vancouver game is the best chance on the slate. The Canucks have the worst expected-goals share, the worst save percentage and the 31st-ranked penalty kill, which is ideal for Utah's power play. San Jose is the trap. The Sharks are outshot and out-chanced most nights, but their goalies sit at +7.3 GSAx, exactly the kind of hot netminder who can steal a game from a team that isn't finishing. Three of four at home against weak opponents should be enough for Utah to stop the slide, even with its own goaltending.

keyMatchups.title: Power play versus Vancouver's kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah's 37.1% power play meets a Canucks kill at 63.5%, 31st in the league, with Vancouver's goalies last in GSAx. This is the likeliest spot for a lopsided Utah win, and the one game where its own goaltending shouldn't matter much.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas shuts down centers
keyMatchups.body: Vegas ranks 1st in holding centers under their expected points and 2nd against all forwards. Utah's offense runs through its middle, so expect a low-event game where Utah's shot edge has to beat a B+ goaltending group. A loss here would be no surprise.

keyMatchups.title: San Jose's hot goaltending
keyMatchups.body: The Sharks are 29th in xGF share and allow 29.8 shots a game, but their goalies rank 5th in GSAx. Utah should pile up chances. Whether it converts against an A- goaltending group is the real question.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Vejmelka or Cossa can post even a league-average save percentage over the homestand. That is the whole gap between this team's play and its results.

restOfSeason.body:
The skaters are a top-five group by process, and that should hold. The power play will cool from 37%, but it has the personnel to stay well above the league's 22.5%. The swing variable is the crease. Team save percentage is far enough below the league, and far enough from last season's positive GSAx, that some recovery is the reasonable bet even without a new goalie. If Utah's goalies merely reach average, a team allowing under 25 shots a game should keep goals against near or below the league's 3.2 and turn its even differential clearly positive.

The downside case is that neither Vejmelka nor Cossa recovers. In that case the weak penalty kill and the goals-against problem keep Utah around a 96-point pace at best, fighting for a wild card in a crowded Central. I expect partial regression toward average in net, which lands Utah roughly 46 wins and 96 points, with real upside beyond that.

projections.stat: Goals allowed / game, rest of season

swingFactors: Team save percentage moving back toward league average
Power play holding most of its early conversion

confidence.note: 18 games is a small sample for goaltending and special teams, but the shot-share edge is large and broad-based.
